newsitem.title: USA: Tax reforms should pass -- Philippines' de Ocampo.
newsitem.headline: Tax reforms should pass -- Philippines' de Ocampo.

text.p: Philippine Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo said he believes his country's Congress will pass proposed income tax reforms, but he repeated that was not a prerequisite for removing International Monetary Fund (IMF) supervision.
"I remain optimistic Congress will pass it (by early June)," de Ocampo said in an interview with Reuters.

That is the month a three-year IMF program expires and IMF officials have said tax reforms would lend the economy to self-sufficiency. The reforms aim to broaden the tax base, streamline collection and improve enforceability.
In their first year, the new rules should add about 14 billion pesos of tax revenue from individuals and corporations, de Ocampo said.
The Philippines could "graduate" from the IMF without passing the tax legislation, but would prefer to enact the reforms first.

"We could do so. Even though we do have (an IMF) program right now, which ends in June, we haven't drawn a single cent from it, because most of our economic targets have been met or surpassed," the Finance Secretary said.
"But the preference, of course, is to exit gracefully," he added.
De Ocampo said exiting the IMF remains an important goal because it would give investors "the perception the economy is doing very well."
Asked about troubled bank Monte de Piedad Savings and Mortgage, de Ocampo said its bad loan portfolio and resulting liquidity crunch did not indicate problems in the overall banking system.

"The banking sector continues to be not only healthy, but prudent, the case of Monte de Piedad notwithstanding," he said. "The case of Monte de Piedad, I think, is an isolated case which involves management decisions that ended up giving that particular bank the difficulties it is presently facing."
De Ocampo confirmed he would run for president in 1998 if endorsed by current president Fidel Ramos.
But speculation mounts that Ramos may seek to amend the Constitution to run for a second term in June 1998.
De Ocampo said he would not oppose Ramos or another candidate endorsed by him.
"I don't think I'd run against the president or his programs," he said.
Asked what he could offer voters, de Ocampo replied: "I'm the only one right now who has the hands-on experience with the economy." ($ = 26.4 pesos)
